claims.claim: A 2021 Cochrane review found no randomised trials of tube feeding in severe dementia, only 14 non-randomised studies; studies of PEG tubes found no evidence that they help people live longer (low-certainty evidence).
claims.supporting_passage: "We found no eligible RCTs. We included fourteen controlled, non-randomised studies. All the included studies compared outcomes between groups of people who had been assigned to enteral tube feeding or oral feeding by prior decision of a healthcare professional. Some studies controlled for a range of confounding factors, but there were high or very high risks of bias due to confounding in all studies, and high or critical risks of selection bias in some studies. Four studies with 36,816 participants assessed the effect of PEG feeding on survival time. None found any evidence of effects on survival time (low-certainty evidence). Three of four studies using mixed or unspecified enteral tube feeding methods in 310 participants (227 enteral tube feeding, 83 no enteral tube feeding) found them to be associated with longer survival time. The fourth study (1386 participants: 135 enteral tube feeding, 1251 no enteral tube feeding) found no evidence of an effect. The certainty of this body of evidence is very low." Plain language summary: "We included 14 studies that included 49,714 participants. Of these, 6203 were tube-fed and 43,511 were not." ... "PEG may make no difference to how long people live (4 studies, 36,816 people)" ... "Studies of people with either PEG or nasogastric tubes showed tube feeding may increase the length of time people live (4 studies, 1696 people)"
claims.location: Abstract, Main results; Plain language summary, What did we find
claims.pico_timeframe: P: adults with severe dementia and poor intake; I: PEG, nasogastric or mixed enteral tube feeding; C: no tube (standard or enhanced oral care); O: survival time; T: varied by study; all observational (allocation by clinician decision)
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review in 2021 found no randomised trials of feeding tubes for people with severe dementia. In 14 observational studies, PEG tubes (a tube into the stomach through the skin) were not shown to help people live longer. The evidence is of low certainty, and a few small studies of other tube types pointed the other way.
claims.qualifications: Say 'not shown to help people live longer' or 'no evidence that', not 'does not prolong life'. All studies were observational, so sicker or different people may have received tubes. Mention that a few small studies of mixed tube types found longer survival (very low certainty) if the post discusses survival in any detail.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Three of four small studies of mixed or unspecified tube methods (310 people) found longer survival; certainty very low. Palecek 2010 notes some studies found PEG survival in dementia similar to other diagnoses. No randomised evidence exists and the review authors think randomised trials would be ethically very difficult.

claims.claim: The American Geriatrics Society does not recommend feeding tubes for older adults with advanced dementia, recommends careful hand feeding, and says tube feeding is a treatment that can be accepted or declined according to the person's wishes.
claims.supporting_passage: "When eating difficulties arise, feeding tubes are not recommended for older adults with advanced dementia. Careful hand feeding should be offered because hand feeding has been shown to be as good as tube feeding for the outcomes of death, aspiration pneumonia, functional status, and comfort. Moreover, tube feeding is associated with agitation, greater use of physical and chemical restraints, healthcare use due to tube-related complications, and development of new pressure ulcers. Efforts to enhance oral feeding by altering the environment and creating patient-centered approaches to feeding should be part of usual care for older adults with advanced dementia. Tube feeding is a medical therapy that an individual's surrogate decision-maker can decline or accept in accordance with advance directives, previously stated wishes, or what it is thought the individual would want."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults with advanced dementia and eating difficulties; US position statement, 2014
claims.safe_wording: The American Geriatrics Society advises against feeding tubes for older people with advanced dementia and recommends careful hand feeding. It says a feeding tube is a medical treatment that can be accepted or declined in line with what the person wanted.
claims.qualifications: US society, 2014. Its comparative statements ('as good as') rest on observational studies. Tube feeding is 'associated with' agitation and restraint: keep the association wording.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with ESPEN 2024 and (by search extract) NICE NG97.

claims.claim: Careful hand feeding ('comfort feeding only') is an individual plan: feed regularly, stop at signs of distress such as coughing or choking, record the foods, techniques and times of day that work; when eating is no longer possible, continue contact through mouth care, talking and touch. It is unlikely to prevent weight loss.
claims.supporting_passage: Palecek 2010 full text: "According to an individualized care plan, she should be fed regularly, with cessation of oral feeding when she begins to show signs of distress (e.g., choking, coughing). Her individualized care plan should document unique signs of distress, which behaviors indicate it is safe to feed, what types of foods are preferable, effective feeding techniques, and at what times of day feeding is preferable. When Mrs. P no longer tolerates oral feedings, the nursing home staff provides an alternative means of positive human interaction, in lieu of feeding, for the remainder of the meal period. Interaction may involve speaking to her and therapeutic touch" ... "In the situation in which the patient is unable to eat without significant distress, the care plan for CFO calls for a form of continued interaction with the resident, which could include assiduous mouth care, speaking to the resident, and therapeutic touch." ... (earlier assessment) "Specific interventions include altering the texture, cohesiveness, viscosity, temperature, and density of Mrs. P's food; changing her posture while eating; environmental modifications; denture adjustment or addressing other dental concerns; and medication adjustment." [reference markers removed] ... (illustrative dialogue) "this order of Comfort Feeding Only places a premium on her comfort during meals but is unlikely to keep her from losing weight." AGS 2014: "Efforts to enhance oral feeding by altering the environment and creating patient-centered approaches to feeding should be part of usual care for older adults with advanced dementia."
claims.location: Palecek 2010 full text: sections 'Reframing the discussion' and 'Managing the care of Mrs. P'; AGS 2014 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Expert description of a care approach for nursing home residents with advanced dementia; not an outcome study
claims.safe_wording: Careful hand feeding means a plan for the person: offer food regularly, stop when they cough, choke or show distress, and write down which foods, ways of helping and times of day work best. Check texture, sitting position, dentures and medicines first. When eating becomes too hard, the mealtime still continues with mouth care, talking and touch. It focuses on comfort and will usually not stop weight loss.
claims.qualifications: This describes an expert-proposed approach, not a tested intervention. The candidate's specific items 'sitting upright', 'small mouthfuls' and 'time' are not in the passages read; use 'changing position', 'effective feeding techniques' and 'preferred foods and times' instead, or source them separately. Include the honest point that weight loss is still likely.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trials of comfort feeding outcomes were identified in this batch.

claims.claim: Declining a feeding tube does not mean stopping food, drink or care; orders to forgo tube feeding are often wrongly read as 'do not feed'.
claims.supporting_passage: Palecek 2010 abstract: "One reason is that orders to forgo artificial hydration and nutrition get wrongly interpreted as \"do not feed,\" resulting in a reluctance of families to agree to them." ... "Comfort feeding only through careful hand feeding, if possible, offers a clear goal-oriented alternative to tube feeding and eliminates the apparent care-no care dichotomy imposed by current orders to forgo artificial hydration and nutrition." AGS 2014: "Tube feeding is a medical therapy that an individual's surrogate decision-maker can decline or accept in accordance with advance directives, previously stated wishes, or what it is thought the individual would want."
claims.pico_timeframe: US nursing home decision-making; expert proposal and position statement
claims.safe_wording: Saying no to a feeding tube is a decision about one treatment. Food, drink, mouth care and company continue, guided by what the person would have wanted.
claims.qualifications: The statement that the decision is 'never about the person's worth' is an ethical position; mark it as judgement ('We should...'), not as a finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: A Cochrane review of 24 studies in people aged 65 and over found that common one-off tests, including fluid intake, urine specific gravity, urine colour, urine volume, heart rate, dry mouth and feeling thirsty, should not be relied on alone to detect or rule out water-loss dehydration; single tests miss many dehydrated people and wrongly label well-hydrated people.
claims.supporting_passage: "We included three studies with published diagnostic accuracy data and a further 21 studies provided datasets that we analysed. We assessed 67 tests (at three cut-offs for each continuous outcome) for diagnostic accuracy of water-loss dehydration (primary target condition) and of current dehydration (secondary target condition)." ... "There was sufficient evidence to suggest that several stand-alone tests often used to assess dehydration in older people (including fluid intake, urine specific gravity, urine colour, urine volume, heart rate, dry mouth, feeling thirsty and BIA assessment of intracellular water or extracellular water) are not useful, and should not be relied on individually as ways of assessing presence or absence of dehydration in older people." ... "Individual tests should not be used in this population to indicate dehydration; they miss a high proportion of people with dehydration, and wrongly label those who are adequately hydrated."
claims.location: Abstract, Main results and Authors' conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: P: people aged 65 and over, various settings; index tests: one-off symptoms, signs and tests; reference: serum or plasma osmolality (or osmolarity or weight change); target: impending or current water-loss dehydration; cross-sectional accuracy
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review pooled data from 24 studies of people aged 65 and over. Urine colour, urine specific gravity, a dry mouth, feeling thirsty, heart rate and recorded fluid intake were each not useful on their own for spotting or ruling out dehydration from not drinking enough. Used alone, they miss many people who are dehydrated and wrongly label others who are not.
claims.qualifications: Applies to water-loss (low-intake) dehydration, not to salt-and-water loss from vomiting, diarrhoea or bleeding. The finding is about single tests used alone; the review suggests combining tests may help. It does not say these observations are worthless as part of a wider assessment.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Few studies per test; some tests were assessed in small datasets.

numbers.meaning: studies (3 published plus 21 datasets analysed by the reviewers)
tests assessed, each at three cut-offs where continuous
pre-set minimum sensitivity and specificity for a test to count as useful

claims.claim: The reference standard was serum osmolality: 295 mOsm/kg or more counted as impending or current water-loss dehydration and over 300 mOsm/kg as current dehydration.
claims.supporting_passage: "Water-loss dehydration was defined primarily as including everyone with either impending or current water-loss dehydration (including all those with serum osmolality ≥ 295 mOsm/kg as being dehydrated)." ... "Diagnostic accuracy of each test was assessed against the best available reference standard for water-loss dehydration (serum or plasma osmolality cut-off ≥ 295 mOsm/kg, serum osmolarity or weight change) within each study." ... "Secondary target conditions were intended as current (> 300 mOsm/kg) and impending (295 to 300 mOsm/kg) water-loss dehydration, but restricted to current dehydration in the final review."
claims.location: Abstract, Objectives and Data collection and analysis
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition used in the review
claims.safe_wording: The review used a blood test, serum osmolality, as its reference: 295 mOsm/kg or more meant dehydration was starting or present, and over 300 meant it was present.
claims.qualifications: Some included studies used osmolarity or weight change where osmolality was unavailable.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: impending or current water-loss dehydration
current water-loss dehydration

claims.claim: Missing drinks between meals and expressing fatigue showed some diagnostic ability in one study of 71 people; no test was consistently useful in more than one study.
claims.supporting_passage: "Only three tests showed any ability to diagnose water-loss dehydration (including both impending and current water-loss dehydration) as stand-alone tests: expressing fatigue (sensitivity 0.71 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.96), specificity 0.75 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.85), in one study with 71 participants, but two additional studies had lower sensitivity); missing drinks between meals (sensitivity 1.00 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.00), specificity 0.77 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.86), in one study with 71 participants) and BIA resistance at 50 kHz ..." ... "No test was consistently useful in more than one study.Combining two tests so that an individual both missed some drinks between meals and expressed fatigue was sensitive at 0.71 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.96) and specific at 0.92 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.97)." ... "Promising tests identified by this review need to be further assessed, as do new methods in development."
claims.location: Abstract, Main results and Authors' conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: One study of 71 older people; one-off assessment against serum osmolality
claims.safe_wording: Only a few signs showed any promise. In one small study of 71 older people, missing drinks between meals was the most promising sign, but it has not been confirmed in other studies.
claims.qualifications: Single small study with very wide confidence intervals (sensitivity 0.59 to 1.00). Present as a promising sign to watch for, not a validated test. Fatigue had lower sensitivity in two other studies.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not replicated; no test consistently useful in more than one study.

claims.claim: In 188 UK care home residents (mean age 86), 1 in 5 were dehydrated on blood testing, and thirst was not associated with hydration status.
claims.supporting_passage: "The Dehydration Recognition In our Elders (DRIE) cohort study included people aged 65 or older living in long-term care without heart or renal failure." ... "DRIE included 188 residents (mean age 86 years, 66% women) of whom 20% were dehydrated (serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg)." ... "Thirst was not associated with hydration status."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 188 UK long-term care residents aged 65+, no heart or renal failure; exposure: thirst and other characteristics; outcome: serum osmolality; cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a UK study of 188 care home residents with an average age of 86, 1 in 5 were dehydrated on a blood test. Whether residents felt thirsty was not linked with whether they were dehydrated.
claims.qualifications: Cross-sectional; excluded people with heart or kidney failure. 'Not associated' is not the same as 'thirst never helps'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with the Cochrane finding for 'feeling thirsty'.

numbers.meaning: care home residents, UK, mean age 86
dehydrated (serum osmolality over 300 mOsm/kg), about 1 in 5

claims.claim: When measured serum osmolality is not available, calculated osmolarity = 1.86 x (Na + K) + 1.15 x glucose + urea + 14 (all mmol/L) was the best of 39 equations in 595 older people across 5 cohorts; at a cut-point of 295 mOsm/L it had sensitivity 85% and specificity 59%, and the authors suggest laboratories report it as a screen.
claims.supporting_passage: Hooper 2015 BMJ Open: "Across 5 cohorts 595 older people were included, of whom 19% were dehydrated (directly measured osmolality>300 mOsm/kg). Of 39 osmolarity equations, 5 showed reasonable agreement with directly measured osmolality and 3 had good predictive accuracy in subgroups with diabetes and poor renal function." ... "The best equation was osmolarity=1.86×(Na++K+)+1.15×glucose+urea+14 (all measured in mmol/L). It appeared useful in people aged ≥65 years with and without diabetes, poor renal function, dehydration, in men and women, with a range of ages, health, cognitive and functional status." ... "Some commonly used osmolarity equations work poorly, and should not be used. Given costs and prevalence of dehydration in older people we suggest use of the best formula by pathology laboratories using a cutpoint of 295 mOsm/L (sensitivity 85%, specificity 59%), to report dehydration risk opportunistically when serum glucose, urea and electrolytes are measured for other reasons in older adults." Siervo 2014: "One [calculated osmolarity = 1.86 × (Na⁺ + K⁺) + 1.15 × glucose + urea +14; all in mmol/L] was characterized by narrower limits of agreement and the capacity to predict serum osmolality within 2% in >80% of participants, regardless of diabetes or hydration status." ... "This equation may be used to predict hydration status in frail older people (as a first-stage screening)"
claims.location: Hooper 2015 BMJ Open Abstract, Results and Conclusions; Siervo 2014 Abstract, Results and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 595 people aged 65+ in community, care home, acute medical, emergency and cirrhosis cohorts (Hooper); 186 UK care home residents (Siervo); index: calculated osmolarity from same blood draw; reference: directly measured osmolality; cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: If measured osmolality is not available, it can be estimated from routine blood results: 1.86 x (sodium + potassium) + 1.15 x glucose + urea + 14, all in mmol/L. This was the best of 39 formulas tested in 595 older people. At 295 or more it picked up about 85 in 100 people who were dehydrated but also flagged many who were not, so it is a screen that prompts a closer look, not a diagnosis.
claims.qualifications: Two figures exist: Siervo 2014 (care homes) reported sensitivity 79% and specificity 89% at 295; Hooper 2015 (5 cohorts) suggested 295 mOsm/L with sensitivity 85% and specificity 59%. Give one set (prefer Hooper 2015, the wider validation) or explain the difference. Units: osmolarity mOsm/L (calculated) vs osmolality mOsm/kg (measured). Other commonly used formulas performed poorly: specify this formula.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Specificity varied between studies and settings.

numbers.meaning: calculated osmolarity equation, all values in mmol/L
equations tested (38 in Siervo 2014)
people aged 65+ across 5 cohorts, 19% dehydrated by measured osmolality over 300
suggested laboratory screening cut-point (Hooper 2015)
agreement with measured osmolality in 186 care home residents (Siervo 2014)

claims.claim: In a population study of 2,491 people aged 53 to 97 in Wisconsin, about 1 in 4 had an impaired sense of smell on testing, rising to 62.5% of those aged 80 to 97; most did not know (self-report detected only 12% to 18% of cases in the oldest group).
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 2491 Beaver Dam, Wis, residents aged 53 to 97 years participating in the 5-year follow-up examination (1998-2000) for the Epidemiology of Hearing Loss Study, a population-based, cross-sectional study." ... "The mean (SD) prevalence of impaired olfaction was 24.5% (1.7%). The prevalence increased with age; 62.5% (95% confidence interval [CI], 57.4%-67.7%) of 80- to 97-year-olds had olfactory impairment. Olfactory impairment was more prevalent among men (adjusted prevalence ratio, 1.92; 95% CI, 1.65-2.19)." ... "Self-reported olfactory impairment was low (9.5%) and this measure became less accurate with age. In the oldest group, aged 80 to 97 years, sensitivity of self-report was 12% for women and 18% for men."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 2491 community residents aged 53 to 97, Beaver Dam, Wisconsin; measure: San Diego Odor Identification Test and self-report; cross-sectional, 1998 to 2000
claims.safe_wording: In a US population study of 2,491 people aged 53 to 97, about 1 in 4 had a weakened sense of smell when tested. Among those aged 80 and over it was about 6 in 10. Most people with a weak sense of smell did not know they had it.
claims.qualifications: One US community (mostly white, Midwest), tested around 2000. 'Most did not know': self-report caught 12% (women) to 18% (men) of those affected in the 80 to 97 group, and self-reported impairment overall was 9.5% against 24.5% measured.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Doty 1984 gives higher figures for ages 65 to 80 (more than half), from a different test and sample; do not give both without reconciling.

numbers.meaning: participants aged 53 to 97, population-based, Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, 1998 to 2000
prevalence of measured smell impairment, all ages 53 to 97 (about 1 in 4)
prevalence among 80 to 97 year olds (about 6 in 10)
self-reported smell impairment, all ages
sensitivity of self-report in women and men aged 80 to 97

claims.claim: In 1955 people aged 5 to 99, more than half of those aged 65 to 80 and more than three-quarters of those over 80 had major impairment of smell identification (Doty 1984).
claims.supporting_passage: "Smell identification ability was measured in 1955 persons ranging in age from 5 to 99 years. On the average, women outperformed men at all ages, and nonsmokers outperformed smokers. Peak performance occurred in the third through fifth decades and declined markedly after the seventh. More than half of those 65 to 80 years old evidenced major olfactory impairment. After 80 years, more than three-quarters evidenced major impairment. Given these findings, it is not surprising that many elderly persons complain that food lacks flavor and that the elderly account for a disproportionate number of accidental gas poisoning cases each year."
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 1955 people aged 5 to 99, USA; measure: smell identification test; cross-sectional; 1984
claims.safe_wording: A 1984 study that tested 1,955 people found major loss of smell in more than half of those aged 65 to 80 and more than three-quarters of those over 80.
claims.qualifications: Old study, sample not described as population-based; tested identification of smells, not flavour at meals. Prefer Murphy 2002 (population-based) as the main figure; if Doty is used, give its date and do not mix its figures with Murphy's. The 'food lacks flavor' sentence is the authors' interpretation, not a measured result.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Murphy 2002 (population-based) found lower prevalence below age 80.

numbers.meaning: people tested, aged 5 to 99
aged 65 to 80 with major olfactory impairment
aged over 80 with major olfactory impairment

claims.claim: Much of what we call the taste of food comes from smell, so loss of smell can make food seem bland.
claims.supporting_passage: Shepherd 2006: "Flavour perception is one of the most complex of human behaviours. It involves almost all of the senses, particularly the sense of smell, which is involved through odour images generated in the olfactory pathway." Schiffman 1997: "Deficits in these chemical senses cannot only reduce the pleasure and comfort from food, but represent risk factors for nutritional and immune deficiencies as well as adherence to specific dietary regimens." Doty 1984: "Given these findings, it is not surprising that many elderly persons complain that food lacks flavor"
claims.location: Shepherd 2006 Abstract; Schiffman 1997 Abstract, Data synthesis; Doty 1984 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Narrative reviews and an interpretive sentence; no measured effect size
claims.safe_wording: The flavour of food depends on several senses, and smell is one of the biggest. A weaker sense of smell can make food less enjoyable and seem to taste of less.
claims.qualifications: No source read gives a percentage of flavour due to smell: do not quantify. Do not say food that tastes of nothing is 'often' a loss of smell; say it 'can be'. Taste loss, mouth problems, illness, low mood and medicines can also play a part.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Link between measured smell loss and reduced food intake in older people was not examined in the sources read.

claims.claim: Loss of taste and smell in later life has several causes: ageing itself, some illnesses (especially Alzheimer's disease), medicines, surgery and environmental exposures; smoking, stroke, nasal congestion and colds are also linked with smell loss.
claims.supporting_passage: Schiffman 1997: "Losses of taste and smell are common in the elderly and result from normal aging, certain disease states (especially Alzheimer disease), medications, surgical interventions, and environmental exposure." Murphy 2002: "Current smoking, stroke, epilepsy, and nasal congestion or upper respiratory tract infection were also associated with increased prevalence of olfactory impairment."
claims.location: Schiffman 1997 Abstract, Data synthesis; Murphy 2002 Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Narrative review (1997) and population cross-sectional associations (2002)
claims.safe_wording: Smell and taste can fade with age, but illness, medicines, smoking and a blocked nose can also cause or worsen it.
claims.qualifications: Murphy's factors are associations from a cross-sectional study. Schiffman is an older review.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Many medicines can dull or distort taste, including some blood pressure medicines, antibiotics and antidepressants; how often this happens is poorly known.
claims.supporting_passage: Doty 2008: "Numerous drugs have the potential to adversely influence a patient's sense of taste, either by decreasing function or producing perceptual distortions or phantom tastes. In some cases, such adverse effects are long lasting and cannot be quickly reversed by drug cessation." ... "In this review, we describe common drug-related taste disturbances and review the major classes of medications associated with them, including antihypertensives, antimicrobials and antidepressants. We point out that there is a dearth of scientific information related to this problem, limiting our understanding of the true nature, incidence and prevalence of drug-related chemosensory disturbances." ... "Unfortunately, stopping a medication is not always an easy option, particularly when one is dealing with life-threatening conditions"
claims.pico_timeframe: Narrative review of drug-related taste disorders, all ages
claims.safe_wording: Many medicines can dull or change taste, including some blood pressure tablets, antibiotics and antidepressants. If food tastes wrong since a medicine was started, ask the GP or pharmacist; do not stop a medicine on your own.
claims.qualifications: The review says the frequency is poorly known, so do not say 'commonly' or name individual drugs as frequent causes. Keep the advice not to stop medicines without advice.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evidence base thin (review authors' own statement).

claims.claim: Trials of adding flavour to meals for older people have had mixed results: in one care home study residents ate more and gained about 1 kg over 16 weeks; a later randomised trial found no change in intake or weight.
claims.supporting_passage: Mathey 2001: "We performed a 16-week parallel group intervention consisting of sprinkling flavor enhancers over the cooked meals of the \"flavor\" group (n = 36) and not over the meals of the control group (n = 31)." ... "On average, the body weight of the flavor group increased (+1.1 +/- 1.3 kg; p <.05) compared with that of the control group (-0.3 +/- 1.6 kg; p <.05). Daily dietary intake decreased in the control group (-485 +/- 1245 kJ; p <.05) but not in the flavor group (-208 +/- 1115 kJ; p =.28). Intake of the cooked meal increased in the flavor group (133 +/- 367 kJ; p <.05) but not in the control group (85 +/- 392 kJ)." Essed 2006: "We performed a single blind randomized 16 weeks parallel study consisting of a control group (n=23), a MSG group (n=19), a flavor group (n=19) and a flavor plus MSG group (n=22)." ... "After 16 weeks, energy intake and body weight did not increase within the control group, the flavor group, the flavor plus MSG group and the MSG group. Between the groups, no differences were found in changes in energy intake and body weight. Enhancing the taste of a cooked meal with flavor and/or MSG does not lead to a higher energy intake and body weight among nursing home elderly. More research is needed to determine the efficacy of flavor enhancement on intake and nutritional status." Schiffman 1997: "Use of flavor-enhanced food can increase enjoyment of food and have a positive effect on food intake and immune status."
claims.location: Mathey 2001 Abstract; Essed 2006 Abstract; Schiffman 1997 Abstract, Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: P: Dutch nursing home residents (67 and 83); I: commercial flavour enhancers (and MSG in Essed) added to cooked meals; C: unflavoured meals; O: intake and body weight; T: 16 weeks
claims.safe_wording: Adding stronger flavours is worth trying, but the evidence is mixed. In one Dutch care home study, residents given flavour-enhanced meals gained about 1 kg over 16 weeks while others lost a little. A later randomised trial by the same research group found no change in how much residents ate or weighed.
claims.qualifications: Both studies were small, in Dutch nursing homes, and used commercial flavour enhancers (and MSG), not herbs, spices or sauces. Tips such as lemon, herbs and pepper are reasonable things to try but are not tested in these trials. Present tips as suggestions.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Direct conflict between the two trials; Schiffman 1997's positive statement predates the null trial.

numbers.meaning: mean weight change over 16 weeks, flavour group (n=36) vs control (n=31), Mathey 2001
residents in the null randomised trial (4 arms), Essed 2006
duration of both trials

claims.claim: EFFORT randomised 2,088 medical inpatients at nutritional risk (NRS 2002 score 3 or more, expected stay over 4 days) in eight Swiss hospitals to dietitian-set individualised nutrition support started within 48 hours, or standard hospital food with no dietary consultation; the trial was open-label.
claims.supporting_passage: "The Effect of early nutritional support on Frailty, Functional Outcomes, and Recovery of malnourished medical inpatients Trial (EFFORT) is a pragmatic, investigator-initiated, open-label, multicentre study. We recruited medical patients at nutritional risk (nutritional risk screening 2002 [NRS 2002] score ≥3 points) and with an expected length of hospital stay of more than 4 days from eight Swiss hospitals. These participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either protocol-guided individualised nutritional support to reach protein and caloric goals (intervention group) or standard hospital food (control group)." ... "In the intervention group, individualised nutritional support goals were defined by specialist dietitians and nutritional support was initiated no later than 48 h after admission. Patients in the control group received no dietary consultation." ... "5015 patients were screened, and 2088 were recruited and monitored between April 1, 2014, and Feb 28, 2018."

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported. Davies 2021 Cochrane: no RCTs, 14 observational studies; PEG not shown to improve survival (low certainty), PEG linked with more pressure ulcers in one study of 4,421 (moderate certainty, the only moderate-certainty finding), no study measured quality of life, one study found no difference in comfort. AGS 2014 does not recommend tubes and recommends careful hand feeding; ESPEN 2024 says tube feeding is not an option in severe dementia or at the end of life. Palecek 2010 (full text) describes what careful hand feeding involves, including stopping at distress, continued contact through mouth care, talking and touch, and that weight loss is still likely. Wording changes needed: the pneumonia finding is inconsistent and ungraded, so it must not be headlined (C13-18-c partly supported); acknowledge that a few small studies of mixed tube types found longer survival (very low certainty); NICE NG97 wording is a search extract only, so it may appear only alongside ESPEN or AGS and should be checked on the live page first; 'small mouthfuls', 'sitting upright' and 'time' are not in the sources read.

Hooper 2015 Cochrane (24 studies, 67 tests, people 65+) supports that urine colour, urine specific gravity, dry mouth, thirst, heart rate and fluid intake should not be relied on individually; single tests miss dehydrated people and mislabel hydrated ones. Reference standard: serum osmolality 295+ (impending or current) and over 300 (current). Missing drinks between meals was promising in one study of 71 only. DRIE: 1 in 5 of 188 UK care home residents dehydrated; thirst not associated. The judge's sharpen request is met: the calculated osmolarity equation 1.86 x (Na + K) + 1.15 x glucose + urea + 14 (mmol/L) was the best of 39 in 595 older people across 5 cohorts (Hooper 2015 BMJ Open; derived in Siervo 2014); at 295 mOsm/L sensitivity 85%, specificity 59%, so it is a screen, not a diagnosis. The post must say the review covers water-loss (low-intake) dehydration, and give one set of accuracy figures for the equation.

Core facts supported, but the angle overstates. Doty 1984 figure is accurate but old and not population-based; Murphy 2002 (population-based, 2,491 people aged 53 to 97) is the better figure: about 1 in 4 overall, about 6 in 10 aged 80+, and most did not know (self-report sensitivity 12% to 18% at 80+). Smell as a major part of flavour is supported qualitatively (Shepherd 2006) but not quantifiably. Medicines that alter taste: supported (Doty 2008), with frequency poorly known. Flavour enhancement trials are mixed (Mathey 2001 +1.1 kg vs -0.3 kg over 16 weeks; Essed 2006 randomised, no effect), and both used commercial enhancers, not herbs or sauces. Not supported: 'often put down to fussiness or low mood' (no source) and 'often a loss of smell' as an attribution; 'mouth problems' affecting taste not sourced in this batch. Coordinate with C14 (senses) to avoid overlap.
candidates.revised_angle: Many older people have lost much of their sense of smell without knowing it: in a population study, about 6 in 10 people aged 80 and over had an impaired sense of smell, and very few of them reported it. Smell is a large part of flavour, so food can seem bland. Things to try (evidence mixed): stronger flavours, sauces, herbs or a squeeze of lemon; ask the GP or pharmacist whether a medicine started recently could be changing taste, and do not stop medicines alone. Open with the unnoticed smell loss or a real question ('Does food still smell of anything to you?'), not with an attribution about fussiness. Say plainly that trials of adding flavour to care home meals gave mixed results.

candidates.reason: Reserve. All essential claims supported from abstracts. EFFORT (Schuetz 2019): 2,088 medical inpatients at nutritional risk, 8 Swiss hospitals, open-label; adverse outcome by 30 days 23% vs 27%, deaths 7% vs 10%; calorie goals reached in 79%, protein in 76%. Age profile confirmed (median 75, IQR 65 to 83; Merker 2020, 1,950 participants). The main outcome was a composite; deaths were one component reported separately (the abstract does not use the word 'secondary', so say 'reported separately'). Key limitation to state: at 6 months deaths were 23.2% vs 24.6% (no clear difference; support stopped at discharge; Kaegi-Braun 2020). Gomes 2019 meta-analysis gives broader context (8.3% vs 11.0% mortality across 27 trials, driven by recent trials). Subgroup of frail or 80+ participants (Baumgartner 2021) supportive but secondary, with a confusing order of percentages in the abstract.

Reserve. Villareal 2017 full text confirms: 160 randomised, 141 completed; all three exercise groups followed the same diet (500 to 750 kcal/day deficit, about 1 g protein/kg/day), so the comparison is between exercise types; weight fell 9% in each; lean mass fell 5% (aerobic), 2% (resistance), 3% (combined); hip bone density fell 2.6% (aerobic), 1.1% (combined), under 1% (resistance, not significant), correcting the candidate's 3%; Physical Performance Test improved 21% combined vs 14% each single. Limitations supported: volunteers able to exercise, cognitive impairment excluded, mostly women, white and well educated, 6 months. ESPEN 2022 English abstract supports: weight-reducing diets only for older people with obesity and weight-related health problems, combined with exercise.
